args.question: I'm Black in this Othello endgame with 10 empty squares left. My legal moves are g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8. Which one gives me the best final disc count assuming my opponent plays well? I calculated c8 flips 6 discs immediately (d8, c7, d7, e6, f5, g4) and b7 flips 5 (c7,d7,e7,f7,g7) - but I know immediate flips don't always mean best long-term result. What's the right move here?

parts.content:
The right move is **b7**.

Why: **b7 is not about the 5 flips now**—it’s about controlling the remaining edge/corner access. It flips along row 7, but more importantly it avoids immediately opening the dangerous lower-left corner structure the way **c8** can. In this endgame, giving White access to corners like **a8/a1/h1** or forcing yourself into bad “next-to-corner” squares is often worse than taking fewer discs now.

So choose:

**Black: b7**.
Alright, going with b7 then - makes sense to prioritize position over just grabbing the biggest immediate flip.

args.question: Ugh, White flipped my b7 back. Now my options are g2, b6, a7, c8. g2 flips 5 discs (f2,g3,g4,g5,g6) which seems like the most. Is g2 still safe long-term, or does it hand White something bad again?

parts.content:
**g2 is not safe**: after Black plays **g2**, White can take the **h1 corner** immediately by playing **h1** and flipping back along the diagonal/line through **g2**. That corner is permanent, so the 5-disc gain can vanish fast.

Here, don’t chase the big flip — the move that keeps Black’s best endgame result is **c8**.

args.question: Only 6 empty squares left (a1, h1, g2, a3, b6, a7), I'm Black with 22 vs White's 36. My legal moves are g2, b6, a7. I noticed if I play g2 (flips 5), White can respond with a3 and flip like 6 of my discs back (a4,a5,b3,c3,b4,b2) - that seems terrible. What should I actually play here to minimize the damage or come back?

parts.content:
Play **a7**.

Reason: **g2** is a big flip, but it gives White the **h1 corner**, which is permanent and also lets White undo a lot of your gain. **b6** also doesn’t solve the corner/edge problem well.

**a7** is the best damage-control move here: it takes edge discs now and avoids immediately handing White that strong corner sequence.

args.question: Now that it's over - I'm still a little fuzzy on why that a3 move worked so well. Can you explain simply why forcing White to pass right there was such a turning point?

parts.content:
Sure. In Othello, if a player has **no legal move**, they must **pass**, and the other player moves again.

That was the turning point because the **a3 move didn’t just flip discs** — it **removed White’s next legal move**. So Black effectively got an extra turn.

In an endgame with only a few empties, that is huge because:

- one extra move = one extra placed disc,
- plus more flips,
- plus you may get to take the last important squares before White can respond,
- and White loses the chance to flip those discs back immediately.

So the key idea is: **a3 won the tempo**. It turned the position from “White replies and undoes your gains” into “White passes, Black moves again, and the game runs out before White can recover.”

Final board count from the image: **Black 33, White 31** — Black wins by 2.

args.question: One more thing I want to understand - earlier you told me not to play g2 first because it'd let White grab h1, but later I did play g2 and White just took h1 for one measly disc and I still ended up winning. Was that first warning overly cautious, or did the board situation actually change by then?

parts.content:
The board situation **changed** — the warning wasn’t just “g2 is always bad.”

Earlier, **g2 first** would have given White **h1 with more empties left**, so that corner could help White control the remaining moves and maybe avoid a pass/tempo loss.

Later, when you played **g2**, White’s **h1**:

- flipped only **one disc**,
- came very late,
- didn’t give White enough mobility,
- and still allowed the key sequence where White had to **pass**, giving Black the extra move.

So the lesson is:

**A corner is powerful, but timing matters.**  
Giving away a corner with 8–10 empties can be fatal; giving it away with only a couple useful moves left may be harmless if you win the tempo/end count.

Final result confirms it: **Black 33, White 31**.

Okay, that clears it up — timing really was the whole trick. Corners aren't automatically fatal to give away, it depends on how many moves are left to exploit them. Good game overall: came back from 20-40 to win 33-31 by winning that tempo battle at the end. Not a bad first outing on one of these puzzles!
